name: Hatshepsut
info: Hatshepsut was the sixth pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt, ruling from c. 1479 to c. 1458 BCE first as regent and then as queen regnant, and is remembered for her trade expeditions and building works.

facts.born: Between 1505 and 1495 BCE; eldest daughter of Thutmose I and his Great Royal Wife, Ahmose, of the Eighteenth Dynasty
facts.died: c. 1458 BCE, presumably in Year 22 of the reign of Thutmose III; the cause is uncertain, a proposed bone cancer resting on a disputed identification of her mummy
facts.role: Great Royal Wife of Thutmose II; regent for Thutmose III from c. 1479 BCE; pharaoh and senior coregent by c. 1472 BCE until c. 1458 BCE
facts.known: ruling as a female king; the expedition to the Land of Punt; the Mortuary Temple at Deir el-Bahari; the Karnak obelisks and Red Chapel; the Speos Artemidos; the later erasure of her monuments

t: Hatshepsut began as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III and by Year 7 of his reign had taken the full royal titulary as senior coregent.
Her reign was a time of prosperity and general peace, marked by the expedition to Punt and hundreds of building projects across Upper and Lower Egypt.
Late in the reign of Thutmose III and under Amenhotep II her statues were destroyed and her monuments defaced, so that she almost disappeared from Egypt's records.
dyk: The Unfinished Obelisk left at its quarry in Aswan broke while being cut for Hatshepsut's 16th year as pharaoh, and it still shows how obelisks were quarried.
ev: On the death of Thutmose II, Hatshepsut becomes regent for the two-year-old Thutmose III
By Year 7 of the reign she is attested as pharaoh, with Thutmose III as junior coregent
In Year 9 an expedition to the Land of Punt returns with 31 live myrrh trees and frankincense
Her last dated attestation as pharaoh, in Year 20 of the regnal count
She no longer appears in Year 22, when Thutmose III begins his first major foreign campaign
Zahi Hawass identifies the mummy KV60A as very likely Hatshepsut, an identification later doubted

sections.early:
Hatshepsut was born between 1505 and 1495 BCE, the eldest daughter of Thutmose I and his Great Royal Wife, Ahmose, in the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. Her father's reign began in either 1526 or 1506 BCE, according to the high and low estimates, though the lengths of the reigns of Thutmose I and Thutmose II cannot be fixed with certainty. Egypt had not long before emerged from the Second Intermediate Period, when the Hyksos occupation had disrupted its trade networks and damaged temples such as the Precinct of Mut at Karnak.

After her father's death Hatshepsut was married to Thutmose II, her half-brother and their father's heir, when she was fourteen or fifteen years old; he was of a similar age. As Great Royal Wife she also held the office of God's Wife of Amun. The couple had at least one daughter, Princess Neferure, whose title "King's Eldest Daughter" suggests that there may have been a second daughter who probably died in childhood. Hatshepsut began building a tomb for herself while she was still queen, on a scale not suited to a pharaoh. Her family is thought to have suffered from inflammatory skin diseases that tend to be genetic.
sections.rise:
When Thutmose II died, the throne passed to Thutmose III, his son by another wife, who was two years old. Early modern scholars thought that Hatshepsut served only as his regent. Modern scholars agree that she first acted as regent from his accession in c. 1479 BCE but assumed the position of pharaoh beside him by Year 7 of his reign, c. 1472 BCE. As queen regnant she shared his regnal count, in effect back-dating her accession to Year 1, and became senior coregent while Thutmose III was relegated to junior coregent.

The earliest evidence of her as pharaoh comes from the tomb of Ramose and Hatnofer near Thebes, where a jar stamped "Year 7" was found with jars sealed for the "God's Wife Hatshepsut" and "The Good Goddess Maatkare", her throne name. Her claim was supported by a story told by priests of her divine birth, in which the god Amun visited Ahmose in the form of Thutmose I, and by the Oracle of Amun, which proclaimed it the god's will that she be pharaoh. Inscriptions in her mortuary temple presented her as her father's appointed successor. According to Kara Cooney, the elite raised her to power because of her record as a high priestess, and gained wealth and power under her rule.
sections.deeds:
Hatshepsut's reign was a period of prosperity and general peace. She re-established trade networks disrupted under the Hyksos and funded a mission to the Land of Punt, which returned by Year 9 with 31 live myrrh trees and luxuries such as frankincense; the expedition was commemorated in relief at Deir el-Bahari, with a depiction of Queen Ati of Punt. Raiding expeditions were sent to Byblos and the Sinai, and it is possible that she led campaigns against Nubia and Canaan, though many Egyptologists have called her foreign policy mainly peaceful.

She was one of the most prolific builders of ancient Egypt, commissioning hundreds of projects in Upper and Lower Egypt. At Karnak she restored the Precinct of Mut, raised twin obelisks that were then the tallest in the world, and built the Red Chapel as a barque shrine. At Beni Hasan she built the rock-cut Temple of Pakhet, later called the Speos Artemidos, whose architrave carries her denunciation of the Hyksos. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, with its focal point the Djeser-Djeseru, is counted a masterpiece of ancient architecture; its architect may have been Senenmut or Hapuseneb. In statues and reliefs she wore the regalia of the office, the Khat head cloth with the uraeus, the false beard and the shendyt kilt, and was shown with masculine traits.
sections.opponents:
Little is recorded of open opposition to Hatshepsut in her lifetime. Her position rested on a series of claims, the divine birth, the oracle and her father's alleged appointment, made because a woman ruling as pharaoh broke with custom; she was the only female ruler to take the office in a time of prosperity. She also broke with tradition by announcing her first heb sed jubilee in Year 15 rather than the 30th year. Jürgen von Beckerath speculated that it marked 30 years since her father's death; Cooney proposed it marked 30 years of the dynasty, or of her own life.

The hostility came after her death. Late in the reign of Thutmose III and into that of his son Amenhotep II, her cartouches and images were chiselled off walls, replaced with the names of Thutmose I or II, smoothed over or covered with new stone; at Deir el-Bahari her statues were smashed and buried in a pit. Early modern Egyptologists took this as a damnatio memoriae driven by resentment. Donald Redford argued that it was political necessity rather than hatred. Joyce Tyldesley suggested Thutmose III wanted succession to run directly from Thutmose II to himself, and with Peter Dorman and Gay Robins that the erasure may have aimed to extinguish the memory of female kingship. Some suspect Amenhotep II, whose own claim was weak, and later research has suggested a routine ritual deactivation of statuary.
sections.last:
Hatshepsut's last dated attestation as pharaoh is from Year 20, c. 1459 BCE. Manetho's figure, given by Josephus, of a reign of 21 years and 9 months points to its end in Year 22, c. 1458 BCE, and a stela at Armant dates the start of Thutmose III's sole rule, and presumably her death, to Year 22. She is no longer mentioned when he undertook his first major foreign campaign that year.

As pharaoh she had prepared a new burial in KV20, probably the first royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings, extended with a new chamber for a double burial with her father, Thutmose I. Under Thutmose III a new tomb was made for him, and her mummy may have been moved to the tomb of her nurse, Sitre In, in KV60. In 2007 Zahi Hawass concluded that the unidentified mummy KV60A was very likely hers, because a molar in a canopic box bearing her name seemed to fit its jaw. Her death was then attributed to bone cancer, perhaps from a carcinogenic skin lotion found in her possession. In 2011, however, the tooth was identified as from a lower jaw while the mummy lacked an upper molar, casting doubt on the identification; a DNA test has been refused because it would destroy the tooth.
sections.legacy:
The erasures almost removed Hatshepsut from Egypt's archaeological and written records. Ancient authors kept a trace: Manetho's queen Amessis or Amensis, called by Josephus the sister of her predecessor, was later identified as Hatshepsut. When 19th-century Egyptologists read the walls of Deir el-Bahari, the bearded king who spoke in feminine nouns and verbs puzzled them, and Jean-François Champollion recorded his astonishment. The resulting confusion over the order of the early Eighteenth Dynasty rulers became known as the "Hatshepsut Problem".

James Henry Breasted called her "the first great woman in history of whom we are informed." Later writers have seen her reign as going against the patriarchal system of her time: she ruled as regent for a son not her own and used the regency to build a female kingship, though only through male symbols of office, which is why she is described as a female king rather than a queen. Her depictions moved from traditionally female forms to mixed and then masculine ones. Her buildings remain her largest legacy: the temple at Deir el-Bahari, the standing Karnak obelisk, the second-tallest ancient obelisk still upright, and the Unfinished Obelisk at Aswan, which shows how obelisks were quarried.

summary: Hatshepsut, daughter of Thutmose I, ruled Egypt from c. 1479 to c. 1458 BCE, first as regent for Thutmose III and then as pharaoh beside him. Her reign brought the Punt expedition and great building works such as Deir el-Bahari, but after her death her monuments were defaced and her name nearly lost.

notes: Birth year: the article gives both c. 1505 (lead) and 'between 1505 and 1495 BC'; start set to -1505 with circa.
The jubilee (regnal Year 15) and the obelisks of her 16th year have no BCE year in the article, so they are in the sections, not the events.
Kara Cooney's three-reign breakdown for the jubilee is in the article; summarised only.
The article gives no figures for the dead of any campaign; campaigns in Nubia and Canaan are only 'possible'.
The article does not say who opposed her in her lifetime; 'opponents' therefore centres on the posthumous erasure and the debate over it.
